After traveling to Beijing, your travels now take you back to the West in the service of the Khan, sending you to the farthest reaches of his empire in search of wealth and fame. Marco Polo II is a standalone game based on The Voyages of Marco Polo, and you don't need the original game to play this one. This new journey will present unique challenges, with new and different actions, new scoring rules, and a new good: rare and valuable Chinese jade. Retread old paths with renewed purpose, or find new ones as you explore farther west, continuing to build the immortal legacy of Marco Polo! Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary For tips on how to play Marco Polo 2, see Tips_MarcoPoloTwo Contents 1 Summary 2 Start 3 Actions 3.1 Guild Seal 3.2 Travel 3.3 Contracts 3.4 Books 3.5 Khan's Favor 3.6 City Action Tiles 3.7 Bonus Actions 3.7.1 Caravans (expansion) 4 End Game Scoring Summary Marco Polo II: In the Service of the Khan is a dice-worker placement game with a heavy contract fulfillment component. The game is played over 5 rounds. Each player will roll their own 5 dice at beginning of the round, then use 1 or more dice to activate various action spaces available on the board -- 1 action per turn, until their dice are all used. (If the sum of your rolled dice is too low, you receive compensation of coins or camels, your choice.) Some black dice can be purchased during turns, to give extra actions for that round only. Players will accumulate and spend resources: coins, camels, black pepper, silk bundles, gold bars, and jade. The pepper, silk, and gold (in order of increasing value) are primarily used to fulfill contracts, while the other resources have multiple uses. For example, camels and coins are often spent to facilitate movement, and jade often used to get better resource income when using the books (market) actions. Jade can be used in place of a coin or a camel, when you're desperate. Camels can be spent to adjust a die value, if you're desperate! All players begin with their meeple(s) in Beijing, in the upper right-hand corner of the board, and move around (leaving a trading post in each new city) in order to gain access to more contracts (5 cities provide them), more action spaces (8 cities provide them), and collect shield icons (particularly those shown on your goal card!), which give you points at the end of the game. Travel along the paths costs coins, camels, and/or jade, as indicated -- and the blue paths require in addition that the player possess a guild seal of the indicated type. Start At the beginning of the game each player will choose a character card and a goal card. These are all unique. Each character has special rules that break some rule of the game. The goal cards specify private goals you can achieve for extra points, divided into two sections. - The top section shows which cities have the indicated shields -- you should try to visit one of each shield. The more unique shields you collect, the more points you will score at the end. The ones on your goal card will count double, if you get them. (There is no benefit to visiting more than one city with the same shield icon.) - The bottom section of the goal card indicates which guild seals you should try to get, and then improve , to score the indicated points. Actions On their turn, a player will select one (or more, as necessary) die and choose a single action space on the board to activate. If an action space fits more than one die, the action requires that many. community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] A gigantic step backwards from Voyages which is a tightly constrained puzzle, with tense gameplay, good interaction and quick!  This is loose, with low interaction, more resources and extra point salad scoring.  I much prefer Voyages1 but it will be a matter of taste, if you like a more heads down efficiency puzzle this might be your jam. + Colourful board draws the eye + Still looks like Marco Polo - This is loose, many options so blocking is limited. - Low interaction - Travel is much easier, no tension and less relevant (just hit the cities you need for your optimised engine)

[Rating: 2/10] Haven't played the first incarnation of the game so can't comment on whether this one is better/worse. It's totally fine for what it is, but what it is isn't terribly exciting - glorified resource conversion with small elements of map movement. Most interesting things here are the various player cards that come with clearly broken special powers...but since they're [i]all[/i] broken, it must be balanced...right? Right?!

[Rating: 2/10] Some of this feels like it's been balanced a little better vs. the original Voyages of Marco Polo, whilst other elements feel more complex just for the sake of it, and it's certainly not something I would teach to someone who has never played VoMP.  As a puzzle to click away at every day or so on BGA I find this is not terrible, but I'm in absolutely no hurry to experience it as a board game.

[Rating: 3/10] Look how they massacred my boy...  Has the same essence as Marco Polo but with extra euro mumbo jumbo bolted on. Now there's a an extra resource with extra conversions! 5 WP spaces that rotate from round to round!           Contracts coming from board spaces is interesting but the new board is awfully busy. There's a level of extra euro chrome that is not interesting to me (just more mental upkeep) when I preferred the tightness and focus of the original.

[Rating: 3/10] Not my type of game, feels more of a chore than game. Strong Euro feeling and this game can be very good for euro game fans. Exploring does not feel like exploring it feels more like a calculated plan, whole game is just about planning, every dice, every round, nothing to realy surprise you, nothing here to enjoy. Arnak is just beter in exploring and does not have crazily unbalanced characters like this game. Avoid this at all cost!
